title: Protein-Losing Enteropathy

content_blocks.text: A disease process characterized by excessive loss of protein into the gastrointestinal (GI)

Protein-losing enteropathy (PLE) may be associated with primary GI diseases (e.g., inflammatory bowel disease, intestinal lymphoma, or intestinal lymphangiectasia) and systemic disorders (e.g., fungal disease or congestive heart failure [CHF]).

Inpatient or outpatient medical management depending on the severity of clinical signs at the time of diagnosis.

With clinical signs due to edema or effusion from severe hypoalbuminemia, albumin transfusion, or colloids (such as hetastarch) may be considered to increase plasma oncotic pressure. Both human and canine albumin can provide a temporary increase in serum albumin, but human albumin transfusion may be associated with adverse reactions in dogs.

If lymphangiectasia is diagnosed or highly suspected, an ultra-lowfat diet, containing 20 g fat/1,000 kcal or less, is indicated. It should be noted that there are currently no commercial diets lower than 20 g fat/1,000 kcal and one study has suggested that an even lower fat content is beneficial.

There is no pharmacologic therapy for PLE itself. Instead, the underlying cause of PLE must be addressed.
However, patients with PLE also lose antithrombin and other anticoagulants and can be hypercoagulable. Thus, patients should be treated with a platelet aggregation inhibitor:

Aspirin and clopidogrel should not be used concurrently.
Clopidogrel should not be used with NSAIDs, phenytoin, torsemide, or warfarin.
Bleeding may be enhanced in patients treated with platelet aggregation inhibitors that have to undergo surgery.

Diuretics such as furosemide (1 mg/kg PO q12h) in combination with spironolactone (1 mg/kg PO q12h) have been used by some clinicians to control edema, pleural effusion, and ascites. However, they do not work consistently in patients with PLE because of decreased plasma oncotic pressure and may be associated

There are anecdotal reports about the use of the long-acting somatostatin analogue octreotide in dogs with PLE, but no clinical trials have been completed to date and no specific dosing regimen has been suggested.

Check body weight, serum albumin concentration, and evidence of recurrent clinical signs (i.e., pleural effusion, ascites, and/or edema). Frequency depends on the severity of the condition. Monitor serum cobalamin concentration if patient was hypocobalaminemic and supplemented with cobalamin.

The primary disease cannot be treated in many cases.
Soft-coated wheaten terriers may have PLN in conjunction with PLE and should be evaluated accordingly.
Some GI parasites have zoonotic potential.
